questions.prompt: Wassim decided a month ago to spend Sunday at the book fair in Sfax. Emna texts him: "Are you free on Sunday?" Wassim: "_____" Emna: "Perfect. See you at the bus station at ten." Which message completes Wassim's turn?

options.text: Yes, and I am going to spend the whole morning there.
Yes, and I will going to spend the whole morning there.
Yes, and I go to spend the whole morning there.
No, I went to the book fair on Sunday morning.

questions.explanation: "Yes, and I am going to spend the whole morning there." completes the exchange: be going to announces an intention already formed before you speak, and Wassim settled his Sunday a month before Emna sent her message. "Yes, and I will going to spend the whole morning there." marks the future twice, with will and with going to, whereas English uses one form at a time. "Yes, and I go to spend the whole morning there." translates the mother tongue word for word and lands on a present simple, which describes a habit and cannot announce a plan. And "No, I went to the book fair on Sunday morning." answers in the past simple about a Sunday that is over, which no question about next Sunday can accept.

questions.prompt: Nizar has to tell his head teacher, by e-mail, that he will not be at Saturday's meeting. Which sentence belongs in that e-mail?

options.text: Hi! No meeting for me on Saturday, sorry about that.
I am afraid I cannot attend Saturday's meeting.
cant make it sat, got smthg else on, sorry :-(
U already know I wont be there on Saturday, right?

questions.explanation: "I am afraid I cannot attend Saturday's meeting." is the one an e-mail to a head teacher requires: full forms instead of contractions, a complete sentence, and the polite opening I am afraid, which softens bad news. "Hi! No meeting for me on Saturday, sorry about that." greets a superior the way you greet a classmate. "cant make it sat, got smthg else on, sorry :-(" belongs in a text message to a friend: shortcuts, a missing apostrophe and a smiley have no place in an e-mail to a school. And "U already know I wont be there on Saturday, right?" writes U for you, forgets the apostrophe of won't, and turns an apology into a question the head teacher now has to answer.

questions.prompt: Mouna's friend has just failed her exam and is in tears. Mouna says: "Don't worry. I'll revise with you every evening until the retake." What is Mouna doing with "I'll"?

options.text: She is describing what she does every evening.
She is reporting a decision taken last week.
She is asking her friend for permission.
She is making a promise at this very moment.

questions.explanation: "She is making a promise at this very moment." is right: will is the form English keeps for something you commit to as you speak, and Don't worry shows that Mouna is answering her friend's distress there and then. "She is describing what she does every evening." reads the sentence as a habit, but a habit takes the present simple, I revise with you every evening. "She is reporting a decision taken last week." would need a plan formed earlier, which English announces with I'm going to revise with you, and nothing in the scene points to one. And "She is asking her friend for permission." mistakes a statement for a question; asking permission would give Shall I revise with you?

questions.prompt: Complete: "Emna's phone had no battery left, ___ she could not read Hedi's message."

options.text: but
since
so
because

questions.explanation: "so" is right: the first half gives the cause, an empty battery, the second half gives what followed from it, and so is the linker that introduces a result — with exactly the comma the sentence already has in front of it. "because" and "since" both introduce a cause, so either of them would turn the sentence upside down and make the unread message the reason why the battery was empty; both would also need no comma in this position. And "but" announces a contrast, whereas there is no opposition here: the second fact follows naturally from the first.

questions.prompt: Mouna writes: "I opened that account in 2016 and I have never changed the password. Nobody worried about security at that time." What does "at that time" point to?

options.text: the moment when Mouna is writing the message
any time in the future, when she changes it
the whole period since she opened the account
the year 2016, when Mouna opened the account

questions.explanation: "the year 2016, when Mouna opened the account" is right: at that time always sends you back to a moment the text has just named, and the only moment named here is 2016. "the moment when Mouna is writing the message" is the exact opposite: now would be written today or nowadays, never at that time. "any time in the future, when she changes it" reads a past marker as a future one, although the verb worried is a past simple. And "the whole period since she opened the account" turns a point into a stretch of time, which would need since then and a present perfect, not at that time with a past simple.
